performers: Pierre Bernac, baritone; Francis Poulenc, piano
intro: Pierre Bernac sings the six Apollinaire songs of Poulenc’s Le Bestiaire, with the composer at the piano. The record, HMV DB 6299, was listed for sale as an import by April 1947.

cues.title: Le Dromadaire
cues.text: The first song sets Apollinaire’s five lines about Don Pedro d’Alfaroubeira, who travelled the world with four dromedaries. The poems come from Apollinaire’s Le Bestiaire of 1911, illustrated by Raoul Dufy.
cues.evidence: Apollinaire, Le Bestiaire, ou Cortège d’Orphée (1911, illustrated by Raoul Dufy), as transcribed on French Wikisource: https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Le_Bestiaire,_ou_Cort%C3%A8ge_d%E2%80%99Orph%C3%A9e, “Le Dromadaire”, p. 16. Graham Johnson, note on Le bestiaire, Hyperion CDA68021/4, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W12466_68021: Poulenc’s six songs are poems 10, 4, 17, 19, 22 and 23 of the collection.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Twelve poems, then six
cues.text: Poulenc chose twelve of Apollinaire’s poems while stationed at Pont-sur-Seine, then cut the set to six on Georges Auric’s advice. He dedicated the six to Louis Durey, who was setting the whole collection.
cues.evidence: Graham Johnson, note on Le bestiaire, Hyperion CDA68021/4, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W12466_68021: the twelve settings at Pont-sur-Seine, the reduction to six on Auric’s advice and the dedication to Durey.

cues.title: La Chèvre du Thibet
cues.text: In the second song the poet says that the hair of the Tibetan goat, even the golden hair Jason took so much trouble over, is worth nothing beside the hair he loves.
cues.evidence: Apollinaire, Le Bestiaire, ou Cortège d’Orphée (1911, illustrated by Raoul Dufy), as transcribed on French Wikisource: https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Le_Bestiaire,_ou_Cort%C3%A8ge_d%E2%80%99Orph%C3%A9e, “La Chèvre du Thibet”, p. 10; the order of Poulenc’s songs follows Graham Johnson, note on Le bestiaire, Hyperion CDA68021/4, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W12466_68021.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: La Sauterelle
cues.text: In the third song Apollinaire’s grasshopper is “la nourriture de saint Jean”, the food of Saint John, and he hopes his verses will be “le régal des meilleures gens”, a treat for the best people.
cues.evidence: Apollinaire, Le Bestiaire, ou Cortège d’Orphée (1911, illustrated by Raoul Dufy), as transcribed on French Wikisource: https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Le_Bestiaire,_ou_Cort%C3%A8ge_d%E2%80%99Orph%C3%A9e, “La Sauterelle”, p. 24; the order of Poulenc’s songs follows Graham Johnson, note on Le bestiaire, Hyperion CDA68021/4, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W12466_68021.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Le Dauphin
cues.text: The fourth song speaks to dolphins playing in a sea whose waves are always bitter. The poet asks whether his joy sometimes bursts out, and adds that life is still cruel.
cues.evidence: Apollinaire, Le Bestiaire, ou Cortège d’Orphée (1911, illustrated by Raoul Dufy), as transcribed on French Wikisource: https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Le_Bestiaire,_ou_Cort%C3%A8ge_d%E2%80%99Orph%C3%A9e, “Le Dauphin”, p. 27; the order of Poulenc’s songs follows Graham Johnson, note on Le bestiaire, Hyperion CDA68021/4, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W12466_68021.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: L’Écrevisse
cues.text: In the fifth song the poet and “incertitude” go away together “à reculons”, backwards, as crayfish do.
cues.evidence: Apollinaire, Le Bestiaire, ou Cortège d’Orphée (1911, illustrated by Raoul Dufy), as transcribed on French Wikisource: https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Le_Bestiaire,_ou_Cort%C3%A8ge_d%E2%80%99Orph%C3%A9e, “L’Écrevisse”, p. 30; the order of Poulenc’s songs follows Graham Johnson, note on Le bestiaire, Hyperion CDA68021/4, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W12466_68021.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: La Carpe
cues.text: The last song asks the carp in their ponds whether death has forgotten them, and calls them “poissons de la mélancolie”, fish of melancholy.
cues.evidence: Apollinaire, Le Bestiaire, ou Cortège d’Orphée (1911, illustrated by Raoul Dufy), as transcribed on French Wikisource: https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Le_Bestiaire,_ou_Cort%C3%A8ge_d%E2%80%99Orph%C3%A9e, “La Carpe”, p. 31; the order of Poulenc’s songs follows Graham Johnson, note on Le bestiaire, Hyperion CDA68021/4, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W12466_68021.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The record in April 1947
cues.text: The Gramophone Shop’s supplement for April 1947 called Bernac’s interpretations “authentic”, recorded with the composer at the piano. It added that Claire Croiza had recorded Le Bestiaire before, on a record no longer obtainable.
cues.evidence: The Gramophone Shop Supplement, April 1947 (Internet Archive), https://archive.org/details/gramophone-shop-supplement-1947-04: the entry for HMV G-DB6299, priced at $2.62 as an imported record.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The Internet Archive item credits Pierre Bernac and Francis Poulenc and lists baritone and piano; the 1947 supplement says “with the composer at the piano”.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: The six songs for voice and piano (Le Dromadaire, La Chèvre du Thibet, La Sauterelle, Le Dauphin, L’Écrevisse, La Carpe); the edition is not stated.
fields.note: The dealer’s supplement lists the six titles and says the composer is at the piano. Johnson’s note gives the six poems as numbers 10, 4, 17, 19, 22 and 23 of Apollinaire’s collection. The printed edition used by the performers is not named.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The record was listed as an import by April 1947 and appears in a numbered list of reviewed records in The Gramophone of September 1947, with a reference to the August issue, p. 34. The session date is not given in the sources consulted.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No source consulted names the studio.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The supplement lists a 12-inch imported record, No. G-DB6299, with Montparnasse on the other side.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The Internet Archive label data read “D.B.6299”; the list in The Gramophone reads “H.M.V. DB6299”.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: 2EA 10804-1 (Le Bestiaire); Montparnasse on the other side, 2EA 10807-1
fields.note: From the item description of this side and of the separate transfer of the Montparnasse side. The take number of the matrix is as given by the transferring archive.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: George Blood, L.P., for the Great 78 Project (Internet Archive); disc from the Bowling Green collection
fields.note: The item description names the engineer’s firm and lists the collections georgeblood and 78rpm_bowling_green.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.value: Not stated; the item was made public on 3 November 2023
fields.note: The public date of the item is an upload date, not the date of the transfer.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Four stylus sizes were tried; the preferred version was equalised with turnover 375 Hz and roll-off −12 dB, and copied under the friendlier file name.
fields.note: As stated in the item description. The published MP3 is the Internet Archive derivative of that file.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Poulenc died in 1963, so the music is in copyright in the EU under the life-plus-70 term, which runs to the end of 2033; national wartime extensions, which can lengthen the term for older works in France, were not assessed. The 1911 text is by Apollinaire, who died in 1918; rights in the poems are not assessed here.
fields.note: Rights in the composition are stated separately from rights in the recording. The United States status of the music is not established here.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: first published before 1963; on sale as an import by April 1947 and reviewed in The Gramophone in 1947.
fields.note: The United States status of a recording made in France in the 1940s is not established.

composer.epithet: Pianist and composer of sacred works, love songs and an opera in which the choir is silenced by the guillotine.
facts: Piano with Ricardo Viñes; counterpoint and composition with Charles Koechlin
Georges Auric · Jean Cocteau · Guillaume Apollinaire · Paul Éluard
Pierre Bernac, baritone; Denise Duval, soprano; Poulenc at the piano
Three operas, songs, choral music, ballets, concertos and wind sonatas
composer.background:
Ricardo Viñes used his feet as well as his hands when he taught the piano. When his pupil Francis Poulenc mishandled the pedal, a buttoned boot prodded his shin. Poulenc remembered the lessons with affection: “I owe him everything,” he told Claude Rostand in their radio conversations of 1953–54. Viñes taught him to make a staccato note sing through the pedal and to distinguish sharply between kinds of touch. Poulenc later adopted his own remedy, in the language of the kitchen, for a meagre piano sound: “Put butter in the sauce!”

He was born in Paris on 7 January 1899. His father Émile ran a chemical business; his mother Jenny came from a family of Parisian artisans and began teaching him piano when he was five. She played Mozart and Schubert, Chopin and salon pieces. Poulenc’s tastes included what he later called “adorable bad music”. His uncle Marcel Royer, known as Papoum, took him to concerts and the theatre. Through the Ballets Russes he came to know Stravinsky, and Debussy’s scores were always in the house. “It is my oxygen,” he told Rostand of Debussy’s music.
